Baryon. Baryons are hadrons composed of three quarks held together by gluon exchange via the strong force. The most familiar baryons are the proton and neutron, which form atomic nuclei. Baryons carry integer or half-integer baryon number, obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, and include exotic particles like the Lambda and Sigma hyperons.

Baryons are composed of three valence quarks bound by gluons. They carry baryon number plus one, while their antiparticles have baryon number minus one. The nucleons are the proton and neutron, the most common baryons in nature. Beyond the nucleons exist hyperons—particles like the Lambda, Sigma, Xi, and Omega—discovered in mid-twentieth century experiments. Baryons may carry spin three-halves or spin one-half depending on their internal quark configuration. Baryon number is conserved in weak and strong interactions. The proton is the lightest and most stable baryon, while the neutron decays with an eight hundred eighty second half-life when free. Exotic baryons called pentaquarks were theoretically predicted and recently observed.

Baryons make up the visible universe. Protons and neutrons form the nuclei of all atoms. The existence of baryons beyond the nucleon was a major discovery of mid-twentieth century particle physics and motivated the quark model itself. Baryon asymmetry—the puzzle of why matter outnumbers antimatter—remains a deep cosmological mystery, yet baryon number remains strictly conserved at high energies.
